3. Diversify supply relationships before the squeeze, not during it.

Congratulations to Alvin Lim, CFA, CMT and Climate Bridge International on a genuine first: Singapore’s first Article 6 Letter of Authorisation, issued by Rwanda.

A couple of reasons this resonates with me.

Rwanda. I’ve seen firsthand atAkagera National Park - Rwanda andNyungwe National Park-Rwanda what happens when the Rwandan government pairs clear rules with long-term partnerships. Capital follows, and results follow capital. This authorisation applies the same discipline to carbon.

Predictability. Globally, more than 348 million credits have been authorised for transfer under Article 6.2, yet only around 150,000 have been delivered. Authorisation is the start line, not the finish. What closes that gap is exactly what this post describes: predictable approvals and risk-sharing that let developers commit capital years before the first credit is issued.

Indonesia is moving in the same direction. Approval timelines are now written into regulation, and our first Article 6 purchase agreement was signed with Norway last week.

The next test is delivery. I look forward to seeing the first issuance.

What does it take to make nature investable?

Our #WALDInnovationFacility discussion at#COP31 brought together government, development finance, project developers, carbon-market standards and investors to tackle that question from different angles.

Four messages stood out:
1. Investment readiness has to be built. Project design, safeguards, carbon and biodiversity evidence, community participation, governance and sound economics all need investment before larger pools of capital can engage.
2. Integrity and investability should reinforce each other. Investing in quality early can reduce downstream risk and strengthen investor confidence.
3. Catalytic finance has a distinct role. Public and concessional resources can finance the difficult preparation stage that markets often cannot.
4. Carbon finance will not always be enough on its own. Some projects will need complementary or blended sources of capital to deliver high-integrity climate, biodiversity and community outcomes at scale.

Many thanks toSandeep Sengupta (IUCN), Friederike Kärcher Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), Jeff Silverman (Conservation International), Liz Guinessey (Verra), Tracy Lane (KPMG Kenya), Joseph Hutabarat (Fauna & Flora Indonesia) and Nicolai Tust (KfW) and participants for a candid, practical conversation, and to Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) andKfW for the partnership withIUCN behind the Facility.

ForWALD Phase II, the direction is clear: build the pipeline, finance integrity early, and generate the evidence needed to move credible nature-based projects from promising concepts towards implementation, investment and scale.

I am pleased to share that we will be presenting our latest case study at the AAPG International Conference & Exhibition (ICE), taking place in Jakarta, Indonesia, on 7–9 December 2026.

Our presentation is titled:
"Enhancing Formation Test Interpretation Using Borehole Image Logs in Heterogeneous Reservoirs, South Sumatra Basin."

What will we share?
Formation testing in heterogeneous reservoirs can be challenging due to lithological variations, fracture-controlled fluid pathways, and limited matrix permeability. These conditions can lead to misleading interpretations, including tight formations, lost seal tests, and unexpected water production.

This study highlights the importance of an integrated subsurface approach in improving formation evaluation and reducing interpretation uncertainties in exploration wells.

Long-term R&D investment + consistent testing + willingness to start small.

In the Age of Digital Marketing and AI, Do Trade Shows Still Matter?

I’m currently at Plastics & Rubber Indonesia 2026, and someone asked me an interesting question:

“Would you still recommend participating in trade shows?”

It got me thinking.

Some of the world’s major plastics exhibitions have surprisingly long histories:

🇺🇸 NPE — 80 years
🇩🇪 K Fair — 74 years
🇨🇳 CHINAPLAS — 43 years
🇮🇳 PLASTINDIA — 36 years
🇯🇵 IPF Japan — 32 years

That’s an average of more than 50 years!

Long before digital marketing, social media, or AI existed, exhibitions were essential opportunities for buyers and suppliers to connect.

Then came the internet, followed by the COVID-19 pandemic, which accelerated digital communication. Now, AI is making information and business interactions even more accessible.

So, do we still need physical exhibitions?

My answer is YES! But their role has changed.

Today, customers can learn almost everything about a company online before visiting its booth.

But can a screen truly replace the experience of standing beside a running machine, hearing its sound, watching products being manufactured, or holding a precisely machined component in your hands?

Can an online meeting recreate the spontaneous technical discussions that happen when engineers and customers stand together in front of actual equipment?

I don’t think so.

It’s like watching New Year’s Eve fireworks online. No matter how impressive the live stream is, nothing compares to standing there, hearing the countdown, and feeling the excitement as fireworks light up the sky.

That’s the magic of being there in person.

Digital tools make it easier to connect, but face-to-face interactions help us truly understand and remember each other.

Of course, exhibiting isn’t always the right choice. It depends on your goals—market development, brand awareness, industry insights, or strengthening customer relationships.

For me, the greatest value of a trade show isn’t simply the number of business cards collected or inquiries received.

It’s those genuine conversations that may become the beginning of a long-term partnership.

Digital marketing and AI haven’t replaced trade shows. They’ve simply changed why we attend them.

What do you think? Are physical exhibitions still worth it?

Enough talking about the magic of being there! Why not experience it together? 🤭

Come find me and let’s create some real memories!

The future of automotive manufacturing will be shaped not just by what we manufacture, but by how deeply we collaborate, innovate and engineer together.

At the TAGMA International Tooling Summit 2026, the panel discussion "From Tool Supplier to Engineering Partner: What Automotive OEMs Will Expect Next” brought together industry leaders to discuss the evolving relationship between automotive OEMs and the tooling ecosystem.

Representing Omega Seiki Mobility, Dr. Uday Narang, Founder and Chairman, Omega Seiki Mobility, shared valuable perspectives on how the rapid evolution of electric mobility is changing the expectations from tooling manufacturers and engineering partners.

As the automotive industry transitions towards electric vehicles, the requirements are becoming increasingly dynamic. Faster product development cycles, evolving vehicle architectures, greater localisation, cost competitiveness and design flexibility are no longer differentiators — they are becoming essential.

A few important takeaways from the discussion:

🔹 From vendors to strategic partners: Toolmakers must move beyond execution and become involved early in product design, engineering and development.

🔹 Engineering-led collaboration: Design-for-manufacturing, simulation and prototyping capabilities will play a critical role in reducing development cycles and improving first-time-right quality.

🔹 The EV opportunity: New vehicle architectures across electric two-wheelers, three-wheelers, LCVs and buses are creating new opportunities as well as challenges for the tooling ecosystem.

🔹 Localisation and innovation: Building stronger domestic capabilities, investing in technology and developing a resilient supply chain will be fundamental to India's manufacturing ambitions.

🔹 Agility and shared responsibility: The ability to manage design changes, tooling costs, intellectual property and delivery timelines through collaborative partnerships will define the next phase of growth.

One message stood out: The next generation of automotive suppliers will not succeed by simply delivering components or tools. They will succeed by becoming an integral part of the OEM's engineering and innovation journey.

It was encouraging to see such meaningful perspectives from distinguished industry leaders, including Mr. B.Thej Kumar, Mr. MITTUL SONI and Mr.Munwar S., with the discussion moderated by Mr. Nishant Kashyap from TAGMA Times andETManufacturing

As India strengthens its position as a global automotive manufacturing hub, closer collaboration between OEMs, technology companies and the tooling industry will be critical to building a competitive, future-ready ecosystem.

In Indonesia, the First Question Is What You Will Build Here

In most Asian markets the first serious question a customer asks is about the product. In Indonesia it is often about you.

What will you build here? Who will you employ? Where is your stock? Who is your partner, and do they have engineers or only salespeople?

It took me a while to stop hearing that as a negotiation tactic. It is policy, and it runs deep.

Indonesia has used local content requirements for years. It has pushed downstream processing of its own resources, from nickel to palm oil. Its B50 biodiesel programme, mandatory since July, keeps more of its palm oil inside its own fuel system. The direction is consistent: add the value in Indonesia.

For a European supplier of process equipment, plastics machinery or biofuel technology, that changes the entry plan. Exporting a machine and flying in for commissioning works once. To stay, you need a local assembly or service partner, a parts stock in the country, and a clear story about which part of your value is created in Indonesia.

That costs more upfront. It also explains why the suppliers who made that commitment years ago are so hard to dislodge.

This week Plastics and Rubber Indonesia runs in Jakarta. Walk the halls and notice who has a local team on the stand, not just a distributor's banner.

If you sell into Indonesia, what did you have to build locally before the business took off?

posts.text:
In the Age of Digital Marketing and AI, Do Trade Shows Still Matter?

I’m currently at Plastics & Rubber Indonesia 2026, and someone asked me an interesting question:

“Would you still recommend participating in trade shows?”

It got me thinking.

Some of the world’s major plastics exhibitions have surprisingly long histories:

🇺🇸 NPE — 80 years
🇩🇪 K Fair — 74 years
🇨🇳 CHINAPLAS — 43 years
🇮🇳 PLASTINDIA — 36 years
🇯🇵 IPF Japan — 32 years

That’s an average of more than 50 years!

Long before digital marketing, social media, or AI existed, exhibitions were essential opportunities for buyers and suppliers to connect.

Then came the internet, followed by the COVID-19 pandemic, which accelerated digital communication. Now, AI is making information and business interactions even more accessible.

So, do we still need physical exhibitions?

My answer is YES! But their role has changed.

Today, customers can learn almost everything about a company online before visiting its booth.

But can a screen truly replace the experience of standing beside a running machine, hearing its sound, watching products being manufactured, or holding a precisely machined component in your hands?

Can an online meeting recreate the spontaneous technical discussions that happen when engineers and customers stand together in front of actual equipment?

I don’t think so.

It’s like watching New Year’s Eve fireworks online. No matter how impressive the live stream is, nothing compares to standing there, hearing the countdown, and feeling the excitement as fireworks light up the sky.

That’s the magic of being there in person.

Digital tools make it easier to connect, but face-to-face interactions help us truly understand and remember each other.

Of course, exhibiting isn’t always the right choice. It depends on your goals—market development, brand awareness, industry insights, or strengthening customer relationships.

For me, the greatest value of a trade show isn’t simply the number of business cards collected or inquiries received.

It’s those genuine conversations that may become the beginning of a long-term partnership.

Digital marketing and AI haven’t replaced trade shows. They’ve simply changed why we attend them.

What do you think? Are physical exhibitions still worth it?

Enough talking about the magic of being there! Why not experience it together? 🤭

In Indonesia, the First Question Is What You Will Build Here

In most Asian markets the first serious question a customer asks is about the product. In Indonesia it is often about you.

What will you build here? Who will you employ? Where is your stock? Who is your partner, and do they have engineers or only salespeople?

It took me a while to stop hearing that as a negotiation tactic. It is policy, and it runs deep.

Indonesia has used local content requirements for years. It has pushed downstream processing of its own resources, from nickel to palm oil. Its B50 biodiesel programme, mandatory since July, keeps more of its palm oil inside its own fuel system. The direction is consistent: add the value in Indonesia.

For a European supplier of process equipment, plastics machinery or biofuel technology, that changes the entry plan. Exporting a machine and flying in for commissioning works once. To stay, you need a local assembly or service partner, a parts stock in the country, and a clear story about which part of your value is created in Indonesia.

That costs more upfront. It also explains why the suppliers who made that commitment years ago are so hard to dislodge.

This week Plastics and Rubber Indonesia runs in Jakarta. Walk the halls and notice who has a local team on the stand, not just a distributor's banner.

If you sell into Indonesia, what did you have to build locally before the business took off?
